children.text: **Updated June 2026:** Malaysia continues to be one of the most English-friendly countries in Southeast Asia for travellers. Here is what has changed and what has stayed the same.
As a tour guide, it’s always fun to watch the amazed and delighted expressions on tourists’ faces when they have their first real experience interacting with the locals.

When it comes to the airport staff and guides, they expect them to speak English, it’s their job, but when they approach a vendor or any random person on the street they prepare to spill out broken sentences backed with exaggerated hand gestures. The Malaysian local smiles and speaks to them in perf
Well, nearly perfect. It’s called Malaysian English.
And the response from the tourist is almost always the same.
“Oh, I didn’t know Malaysians can speak such good English!

” Yes, Malaysians do speak English, so don’t be shy to go ahead and speak as you normally would and they will reply to you in Malaysian English. Of course, there will be some differences in the usage of words, perhaps phonetics and a little Malaysian flare will be added in. But these types of differ

So this is where it might get a little confusing. Malay is the official national language of Malaysia, which is broken up into ten dialects. The earliest known record of Malay is found on inscriptions in southern Sumatra and on the island of Bangka, and dates back to 683-6 CE. At that time it was written in Indian script and heavily influenced by Sanskrit. It was transformed in the 14th century to Arabic, then again in the 17th century t

By the mid-18th century, the British had set up trading posts on the Malay peninsula. With them, they brought politics, goods for trade and English. Since 1819, the British already had control of Singapore and English began to have an influence on the Malaysian language, and vice versa. Words like p
The English used in Malaysia today is based on British English and is called Malaysian English. They follow British spellings, however, American slang is strong, especially among Malaysian youth.

Like Malay, English plays an important role to bridge the gap between dialects and languages, such as among Chinese or Tamil speakers, so they can communicate comfortably. When talking to people who don’t understand their language, they will instead use Malay, English or a mixture mentioned before,

Manglish shouldn’t be confused with Malaysian English. Even though they may have similar names, unlike Malaysian English which follows the rules with some local flare added, Manglish doesn’t always follow the grammatical structure of British English.
Manglish also has influences from other languages as, Hokkien, Mandarin, Cantonese, and Tamil.
Take note: As with any country and language, Manglish can vary from region to region in its usage and slang according to certain influences.
Understanding “la” is fundamental. It can be used in a variety of ways in daily communication and describes different kinds of emotions, but it really has no specific meaning.
• Frustration - what la
• To emphasize - ya la
• Feeling so so - OK la
• Trying to chill - come on la
• To ask - serious la?
• Denying - no la
Example:
You to the vendor: Can you give me a discount?
In Manglish: Ei, cheaper la!
There’s no definite answer to where the usage of “la” came from, however, the Chinese do make use of “lah” and lay claim to its influence.

Only used with males, it literally means what it’s supposed to mean, but here in Malaysia, it’s widely used as a sign of respect or to make someone feel important. Example:

This one can be confusing. No pun intended. When a local uses the word “one” they aren’t referring to the number. It’s used more for emphasis.

Meaning: So handsome! Going out with a girl?

This isn’t what you would think it is. This is not referring to a person who likes to spend lavishly on things they don’t need. No, in our local lingo spender means a male’s brief. Yes, you read correctly. Spender is underwear. I don’t think an example is really needed here.

If you hear a local saying he wants to tackle a girl, please don’t call the police. In Manglish, “tackle” means to get a girl’s attention.

Here are some examples of how Malay words are used in conjunction with English.
Tapau means to take away or pack up the food.
Example:

Bos, tapau chicken rice, can?
This word comes from Cantonese and means “to settle” as in to finish some work or to settle a problem.
Example:

Lee: Don’t worry boss. I will kautim it for you. Other interesting words you may hear:
This word is referring to westerners, but not in a derogatory way.
Example:
Local (to the taxi driver): Tolong jap tunjuk Mat Salleh tu macam mana nak gi Kuantan.
Meaning: Please help to assist the westerner, he wanted to go to Kuantan.
Jambu’s original meaning was supposed to be a guava fruit but has been transformed to refer to a cute boy like the author of this article and Korean boy bands.

Tamil is another popular language used by the Indian-Malaysians. Sinhalese is a language mainly by the Sri Lankan population and Thai is spoken in some parts but is considered a minority language.
There are over 30 native tribes in Malaysia each with its own unique ancestral language including sub-dialects. Kazadandusuns and Iban are the most recognizable among the native languages.

Don’t feel pressured to learn a whole new language before your vacation. Although the locals do appreciate the respect for their mother tongue, they are always more than happy to practice their English with a real westerner.

English is widely spoken in Malaysia, particularly in urban areas like Kuala Lumpur and Penang. It is a compulsory subject in all schools and used in business, legal, and medical settings.

In smaller towns and rural areas, English proficiency is lower. Learning a few basic Malay phrases like "terima kasih" (thank you) and "berapa" (how much) goes a long way.

Manglish is Malaysian Colloquial English, a blend of English with Malay, Chinese dialects, and Tamil. You will hear it in everyday conversation. It is friendly and informal, and most speakers can switch to standard English when needed.

Nobody searches "durian" because they want a fact sheet. They search because they are standing in front of a pile of spiky green footballs at a roadside stall in Penang, the seller is gesturing at them in Hokkien, and they have absolutely no idea wha

What Eating Durian Actually Feels Like

The first time I ate durian, I was at a stall outside Balik Pulau. The seller  -  an uncle in a singlet who had been selling durian since before I was born  -  picked up a fruit the size of a rugby ball, sniffed the base, and shook it next to his ear lik

The smell hit first. Sweet and sulfurous  -  like caramelised onions and overripe mango and something else, something that does not have a name. It fills the space around you. There is no pretending you are not eating durian.

The texture is custard. Not "custard-like." Actual custard. A good Musang King is the consistency of thick crème brûlée with threads of fibre running through it like the strings in a perfectly ripe mango. It coats your mouth. It is warm  -  durian gene

This is the experience section. It exists because Google's EEAT guidelines reward first-hand experience over research. But it also exists because you cannot write about durian without describing what it feels like to eat one. If you skip this, you ar
How to Choose a Durian (The Method)

**Step 1: Sniff the base.** The base of the durian  -  the flat end opposite the stem  -  should smell strongly sweet. No smell means unripe. A sour or fermented smell means overripe. The uncle at the stall will do this for you if you ask. Let him.

**Step 2: Shake it.** Hold the durian with both hands and shake gently. You should feel the seeds shifting inside. If they are completely still, the fruit is too firm. If they slosh, it is waterlogged. A slight movement is perfect.

**Step 3: Know your variety.** Memorise exactly three names. Musang King (sweet, creamy, expensive). D24 (bitter, complex, the connoisseur's choice). Kampung (wild, unpredictable, cheap, the one locals actually eat at home). You do not need to know a

**Step 4: Let the seller open it.** Do not try to open a durian yourself. You will either fail and look foolish, or succeed and get durian thorn in your palm, which hurts more than you would think. The seller opens it with a single fluid motion that
What Durian Means to Malaysians

In 2023, a single Musang King sold at auction for RM 8,888. A Malaysian dentist bought it. This is not about the fruit. This is about status, obsession, and the fact that durian is the closest thing Malaysia has to a national religion.

Malaysians do not just eat durian. They drive two hours to a specific farm in Raub because that farmer's Musang King won a taste competition in 2019. They argue about D24 versus Red Prawn with the intensity of football fans. They judge you  -  silently

If you tell a Malaysian you like durian, they will immediately ask which variety. Have an answer ready. "Musang King" is safe. "D24" is more interesting  -  it shows you have been paying attention. "I like whatever is in season" is the correct answer i
What Tourists Get Wrong (And What to Do Instead)

**Mistake 1: Eating durian in a hotel room.** Most Malaysian hotels ban durian. The smell lingers for days and seeps into curtains, carpets, and your neighbour's patience. Eat it at a roadside stall where the seller opens it for you and provides plas

**Mistake 2: Pairing durian with alcohol.** Durian contains sulphur compounds that slow down alcohol metabolism. You will get drunker faster and feel terrible the next day. Drink water. Drink coconut water. Do not drink beer.

**Mistake 3: Buying pre-packaged durian from a supermarket.** Pre-packaged durian has been opened for hours. The flesh has oxidised. The texture has degraded. The smell has faded. You are paying a premium for a pale imitation. Buy whole fruit from a
Where to Eat Durian in Malaysia

**Penang  -  Balik Pulau.** This is durian country. The hills behind Balik Pulau produce some of the best durian in Malaysia, including the rare Black Thorn variety. Stalls line the road from June to August. Go early  -  the good ones sell out by 11am.

**Pahang  -  Raub.** Musang King territory. Raub's soil and elevation produce fruit that auctioneers describe the way wine critics describe Bordeaux. It is a two-hour drive from KL. Worth it. Plan a morning trip and be back before the afternoon rain.

**KL  -  Jalan Alor at night.** Not for buying whole durian. For eating it fresh at a stall while the city buzzes around you. The durian sellers on Jalan Alor know tourists. They will help you choose. Let them.

If you want someone to handle the choosing, the opening, and the explaining  -  Simply Enak runs food tours in KL that include durian tasting at stalls where the seller knows his fruit like a sommelier knows his wine list.
FAQ
**Which durian variety is best for beginners?**
Musang King. It is the sweetest, creamiest, and most approachable. D24 is for people who have already decided they like durian and want to explore the bitter end of the spectrum.
**When is durian season in Malaysia?**
Main season: June to August. Second smaller season: December to January. Prices are lowest in June and highest in late July when the Singapore weekend rush hits.
**How do I get the smell off my hands?**

Pour water into the empty durian shell, swish it around, and wash your hands with it. This is the traditional method and it actually works better than soap. The shell neutralises the sulphur. Then wash with soap.
**Can I bring durian on a plane?**
No. No airline in Southeast Asia allows durian in the cabin or checked luggage. The smell permeates the cargo hold. Eat it before you fly.
